scenes.title: Where and when
narration: The riel is considered one of the oldest entertainment forms used as a social, cultural, and educational tool by the Khoisan people long before Western cultures arrived at the Cape of Good Hope.
Originally danced by Khoisan hunters around campfires after hunting expeditions or harvests, it absorbed distinct Irish and Scottish folk music influences alongside Dutch folk songs.
Over time, the native Khoisan languages mostly disappeared, and the Afrikaans word 'riel' was borrowed from the Scottish 'reel'.

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: Originally danced during celebrations after hunting expeditions or good harvests, the rieldans acts as a narrative tool for romance, animal observation, and community solidarity.
It portrays wooing and lovemaking through animal courtship rituals, as well as the daily working environment of sheep shearers, herdsmen, and farm laborers.
Today it is a living tradition.

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: Danced at an energetic, frantic pace, the rieldans relies on intricate, fast footwork meant to kick up dust in the sand, giving rise to the phrase 'Dans lat die stof so staan'.
Performed by groups often in a circle, the choreography consists of cultural gestures that tell stories of wooing, courtship, and daily labor.

Dancers imitate animal and bird movements—such as the ostrich, butterfly, antelope, baboon, snake, meerkat, and strutting horses—using techniques like 'bokspring' (gamboling), trotting, and 'kapperjol'.
Watch for vlerksleep, askoek slap, bokspring.

scenes.title: Listen
narration: Rieldans features lively music influenced by Irish and Scottish folk music, Dutch folk songs, minstrel tunes, and boeremusiek.
Instrumentation combines traditional and handmade working-class instruments.
Listen for the ramkie (tin oil-can guitar), handmade violin, accordion, mouth organ.
Lively boeremusiek featuring fast acoustic accompaniment led by the distinctive metallic resonance of the tin-can ramkie, accordion, and mouth organ.

scenes.title: The costume and the setting
narration: The dance was traditionally performed in the dusty sand around a campfire, and modern competitive performances retain dusty floor settings to highlight the kicking up of dust.
Costumes are bright and colorful to portray the prancing of animals, while reflecting traditional working-class farm clothes.
For male dancers, the hat is a crucial accessory used during courtship gestures to win a lady's hand in marriage.

scenes.title: The people
narration: The Nuwe Graskoue Trappers, a famous rieldans troupe and orchestra from Wupperthal, brought international prominence to the dance in July 2015 at the World Championship of Performing Arts in Los Angeles, winning 14 gold and eight silver medals in the senior dance category, alongside seven silver medals and an open dance trophy won by their musical band.
The dance is known as Ikhapara by the Nama people, derived from the word 'khapas' meaning hat.

Originating from ancient Khoisan hunter-gatherer campfire traditions, the dance integrated Scottish and Irish reel elements and Western colonial instruments (guitar, violin) while maintaining traditional storytelling, animal mimicry, and working-class heritage.
